readerTitle: 'Not right now' is rarely about the calendar
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주택 도장업체, 사무실 청소 계약) + 실제 연구 (현상 유지 편향, Samuelson & Zeckhauser 1988)
insight: '지금은 아니에요'는 날짜가 아니라 우선순위에 대한 말이다. 무엇이 바뀌면 '지금'이 되는지를 물어야 한다.
misconception: '지금은 아니에요'라는 말을 들으면 정중하게 물러나 나중에 다시 연락하거나, 할인으로 당장 결정하게 만들면 된다.

sources.text: Samuelson, W. & Zeckhauser, R. (1988). Status Quo Bias in Decision Making. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 1(1), 7–59.
도장업체와 청소 계약 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Samuelson & Zeckhauser(1988)의 핵심 결과(선택지 중 하나가 '현재 상태'로 제시되면 사람들이 그것을 더 자주 고른다)를 카드 5에 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 구체적 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
'결정 안 함(no decision)'으로 잃는 거래 비율에 대한 업계 통계는 출처마다 차이가 커서 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: 'Not right now' is rarely about the calendar
body: A house painter walks a homeowner through a quote for the outside of her house. She nods, smiles and says, "This looks great. Just not right now. Maybe in spring."
He writes *call in spring* in his notebook and leaves feeling good. It is one of the most common things a seller hears. It is also one of the most misread.

image.label: Painter leaving a house, notebook reading 'call in spring'
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 겨울 오후, 페인트공이 집 현관에서 웃으며 나오고 손에 든 수첩에 "call in spring" 메모. 창문 안쪽의 집주인은 살짝 고민하는 표정. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: You're the painter. What do you say?
body: The homeowner liked your work samples and didn't push back on the price. She just said, "Not right now."
What's your best reply?

options.text: "I can take 10% off if you book this week."
options.feedback: A deadline might win the job. But you give up margin without knowing what was actually holding her back, and she may now expect a discount every time.

options.text: "No problem. I'll give you a call in spring."
options.feedback: Polite and low-pressure. But you leave without knowing why spring, so your spring call will be a guess.

options.text: "Makes sense. What would make spring a better time than now?"
options.feedback: You accept her answer without arguing, and you learn what is really in the way. It takes a little nerve to ask.

cards.title: The spring call came too late.
body: In April the painter called. The house had already been painted in March by someone her neighbor recommended.

Spring had never been the real reason. She wasn't sure about the color, and her husband thought the old paint could last another year. The neighbor's painter brought color samples to the door and answered his questions.
The first painter lost the job without ever learning what the objection was.

cards.title: 'Not now' is a ranking, not a date.
body: When customers say **"not right now,"** they usually mean: *this isn't more important than everything else on my list yet*, or *something is blocking me that I haven't said*.
Sometimes the timing is real: cash arrives next quarter, a move is coming. Often it hides a doubt, another decision-maker, or fear of the hassle.
Your job isn't to beat the objection. It's to find out which kind it is.

image.label: A to-do list where the offer sits below other priorities
image.brief: 손글씨 할 일 목록 일러스트. "Kids' school fees", "Fix car", "Holiday" 아래에 "Paint house"가 놓여 있고, 그 옆에 작은 물음표 쪽지들("Color?", "Husband?")이 붙어 있음. 달력 아이콘은 흐리게 처리.

cards.title: Your real rival is doing nothing.
body: In a 1988 study, economists William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser found that people pick an option more often when it is presented as the **status quo**, the way things already are.
Keeping the old paint, the old supplier or the old habit needs no decision. Changing does. So "later" is the easy answer, and later tends to keep moving.
That's why a vague follow-up rarely works. Nothing has changed by the time you call.

cards.title: Turn 'later' into something specific.
body: A good reply has a few steps, in roughly this order:
list: **Agree first:** "That makes sense." Arguing makes people defend their delay.
**Ask what changes later:** budget, a person, an event?
**Ask what would need to be true** for them to say yes.
**Tie the next step to a trigger,** not just a date: "I'll bring samples once you've talked it over."
**Offer a small first step** if the change feels big.
cards.callout: If you can't name what will be different later, later probably won't come.
cards.softwareNote: "Not this quarter" often means the buyer lacks budget approval or fears a messy switch. Ask who signs off and when the current tool renews, then offer a small pilot before that date.

cards.title: Sometimes 'not now' really means no.
body: Some people say "not right now" because it is kinder than "no." Asking once is useful. Asking three times feels like pressure and burns goodwill.
And some timing is genuine. If the customer's money truly arrives in March, a fake deadline only teaches them not to trust you.
If your questions reveal a clear no, accept it gracefully. That is a skill of its own.

cards.title: Now it's an office cleaning contract.
body: You run a commercial cleaning company. An office manager says, "Not right now. We're under contract with another company until autumn."
What do you do?

options.text: "Can I send you a reminder in September?"
options.feedback: It respects the contract and keeps the door open. But you don't know if she's unhappy or who decides, so September starts from zero.

options.text: Ask what they'd want done differently, who decides on renewal and when, then offer a one-off deep clean before then
options.feedback: You learn the real trigger and the real decision-maker, and a small paid job lets them try you. It takes more effort than a reminder.

options.text: "Switch now and we'll cover your cancellation fee."
options.feedback: It might win the account. But you pay to solve a problem she never said she had, and you start the contract at a loss.

cards.title: Find out what 'later' is waiting for.
body: "Not right now" is a statement about priorities. Agree, then ask what would have to change, and attach your next step to that change.
**Try it today:** look at your last three "not now" answers. For each, write down what you think would make it "now." If you don't know, that's your next call.
